Best self-hosted Google Photos alternatives (2026) | opentools.dev Skip to content If you want something that feels like Google Photos, with automatic phone backup, face recognition and a timeline, Immich is the closest open-source match today. PhotoPrism is the better pick if you already have a big photo archive on disk and want to browse and search it. Ente is the one to look at if end-to-end encryption matters most to you.
 The other apps in this list are more specialised: Lychee and PiGallery2 are galleries for showing photos, not backup tools for your phone.
 What to look for
 Google Photos does several jobs at once, and the self-hosted apps split them differently. Before you choose, decide which of these you actually need:
 Phone backup: an app on your phone that uploads new photos in the background. Without it, you need a separate sync tool.
 Search and faces: finding "beach" or a person's face across years of photos needs machine learning, and machine learning needs RAM and CPU.
 Sharing: albums for family, public links for friends, several user accounts.
 Your existing archive: some apps want to own the photo folder, others index a folder you already have and leave it alone.
 Quick comparison

 PhotoPrism Via the web app (PWA) or WebDAV Yes Organising an existing archive AGPL-3.0 about 40,000 
 Ente Yes, official apps Yes, on the device End-to-end encryption AGPL-3.0 about 29,000 
 LibrePhotos Mobile app listed in the repo Yes Tinkerers who like a smaller project MIT about 8,100 
 Lychee No Not mentioned Publishing albums on the web MIT about 4,300 
 PiGallery2 No Not mentioned Read-only gallery on a Raspberry Pi MIT about 2,300 
 Immich
 Immich describes itself as a photo and video backup solution directly from your phone, and that is where it is strongest. The official mobile apps back up selected albums automatically, also in the background. The web app and the phone apps both have face recognition, maps, shared albums, multiple users and "memories" from past years.
 It is also the most active project here by a wide margin: about 116,000 GitHub stars and more than 200 commits in most months of the past year, with v3.3.1 released on 8 October 2026.
 The cost is hardware. Immich's requirements page asks for at least 6 GB of RAM and 2 CPU cores, and recommends 8 GB and 4 cores. With 4 GB it can run if you turn off machine learning, which also turns off smart search and faces. The Postgres database should sit on a local SSD, never on a network share.
 One thing to understand about backups: Immich's database holds only metadata and user information. Your actual photos are in the upload folder, and you need to back up both.
 It suits anyone who wants to cancel Google Photos and keep the same habits. Run it on your own server with Docker Compose (the docs have a ready-made file), or on a managed host such as blitz.cloud, where Immich installs in one click Ad .
 PhotoPrism
 PhotoPrism comes from the other direction. It is great at indexing a large folder of photos you already have, tagging them and making them searchable, with faces, places and an interactive world map.
 It runs on less hardware than Immich: the docs ask for at least 2 cores and 3 GB of RAM, plus 4 GB of swap. Face recognition is turned off on systems with 1 GB of memory or less.
 There is no native phone app. You can install the web app on your phone as a progressive web app, or upload through WebDAV with a sync app.
 PhotoPrism also has paid editions. The free Community Edition has fewer account roles (Super Admin, Admin and Guest), while Essentials and Plus add more roles, and Plus adds a user management interface. OpenID Connect single sign-on is listed for the paid editions only. For a family where everyone shares one library this rarely matters, but check the editions page if you plan several separate users.
 It suits people with a big existing archive who care about browsing and search more than about phone backup.
 Ente
 Ente is a photo service with end-to-end encryption, and its whole stack, including the server, is open source. Ente says the self-hosted server is "the same code we use on production."
 That makes it unusual: the official Ente Photos apps for Android and iOS back up in the background, and you can point them at your own server. Face detection and grouping happen on the device, which is how it works with encrypted photos the server cannot read.
 Self-hosting starts with a quickstart script that creates a Docker Compose setup. The minimum listed is 1 GB of RAM and 1 CPU core, and Docker runs the object storage for the photos as one of the services.
 It suits people who want encryption even from the server admin, or who like Ente's hosted service but want the option to run it themselves.
 LibrePhotos
 LibrePhotos is a smaller, MIT-licensed project with a feature list that reads close to Immich: face detection and clustering ("name a person once and the rest is suggested"), object detection, semantic search, multiple users, shared albums and a map. Its repo lists an offline-first mobile app for Android and iOS built with Expo.
 The recommended install is a single Docker container that serves the API and web app together. With about 8,100 stars, its community is much smaller than Immich's, so expect fewer guides and slower answers.
 It suits people who prefer an MIT-licensed project or want to try a smaller alternative.
 Lychee
 Lychee is a photo management and publishing tool. You upload photos from your computer, a server, a URL or Dropbox, put them in albums, protect albums with passwords or make them public in one click.
 Lychee does not mention a phone backup app or face recognition. That is fine, because Lychee solves a different problem: showing photos to other people in a clean web gallery. There is a docker-compose file for setup and a paid Supporter Edition to fund the project.
 It suits photographers and families who want to publish albums, alongside a separate backup tool.
 PiGallery2
 PiGallery2 is a "directory-first photo gallery website" made for low-resource servers, especially the Raspberry Pi. It is read-only: "Your photo folder is never modified." You point it at a folder and get a fast web gallery on top. Docker is the recommended way to run it.
 It suits someone with photos on a NAS or a Pi who wants to browse them in a browser without any app touching the files.
 Two more worth knowing
 If you already run Nextcloud , the Memories app adds a photo timeline on top of the files you sync there, with face tagging through Nextcloud's recognition apps. Photoview is another gallery that indexes existing folders.
 How to run them
 All of these are self-hosted, so the usual three routes apply:
 Your own server with Docker. A home server is the natural place for a photo library because disk space is cheap there. Immich and PhotoPrism both publish official Docker Compose files.
 A rented server. Works well, but storage for many years of photos adds up. Check disk prices before you move 500 GB of videos.
 A managed host. Immich is available on blitz.cloud, where it installs in one click with HTTPS, hosted in the EU. There is a free plan without a credit card; apps on it sleep after 30 minutes without visitors.
 Whatever you choose, keep a backup outside the app. Our self-hosting for beginners guide explains how to plan for that.
 FAQ
 What is the best self-hosted alternative to Google Photos?
 For most people Immich, because it has official phone apps with background backup, face recognition and sharing, and the most active development. PhotoPrism is a strong second if you mainly organise an existing archive.
 Can I import my Google Photos library?
 Yes, through Google Takeout, which exports your photos with metadata in separate JSON files. For Immich, the docs recommend a community-maintained tool called immich-go to import a Takeout archive. Test with a small part of your library first.
 Which option runs on a Raspberry Pi?
 PiGallery2 is built for it. Immich needs at least 6 GB of RAM for a smooth experience, so it only fits on the larger Pi models, and without machine learning features on smaller ones.
 Is there an end-to-end encrypted option?
 Ente. Its apps encrypt photos on your device before upload, and you can self-host the server.
 Do these apps replace a backup?
 No. They are where your photos live, which makes them the thing you back up. Keep at least one more copy elsewhere.

Best Google Photos Alternatives in 2026 | Independent Editorial Guide
 Recommendation 
 Updated September 2026 
 · 
 ~19 min
 read 
 Why people are actually leaving Google Photos
 Most guides to this topic open with a vague warning about "big tech"
 and move on. The real reasons people leave are more specific, and
 worth naming, because they change which alternative actually fits
 you. Google ended unlimited free storage for photo backups back in
 2021, so most active users are already paying for a Google One plan
 whether they meant to or not. Photos, Gmail attachments, and Drive
 files all draw from the same storage pool, so a phone that backs up
 in the background can quietly fill that pool without anyone noticing
 until the "storage full" email shows up. And Google's photo indexing
 the face grouping, the "on this day" memories, the searchable
 "beach" or "receipt" queries runs on your images whether or not you
 use Google's other products, which is the part that bothers
 privacy-conscious users most.
 None of that makes Google Photos a bad product. It's genuinely good
 at what it does: reliable background upload, solid search, and an
 interface most people never have to think about. The tools below
 aren't trying to be a straight clone of it. Some trade a bit of that
 polish for you owning the storage outright. Others keep the "just
 works" feel but encrypt everything so the provider can't read your
 library even if they wanted to. Which one is right for you depends
 less on features and more on how much responsibility you're willing
 to take on.
 Transparency: Some links below are affiliate
 links. We may earn a commission at no extra cost to you. Sponsored
 placements never change editorial order.
 Read our sponsorship FAQ .
 Tools without an affiliate program link straight to the vendor or
 our directory .
 What to actually evaluate
 Who can technically access your photos — a
 self-hosted tool means only you; an encrypted cloud service means
 the provider stores ciphertext it can't read; a regular cloud
 service (including Google) can technically access files unless you
 add your own encryption layer.
 Automatic mobile backup — the single feature that
 makes or breaks whether you'll actually stick with a new tool. If
 backup isn't automatic, most people quietly stop using it within a
 month.
 Face recognition and search — useful, but it's
 also the most compute-heavy feature, so it's the first thing that
 suffers on underpowered self-hosted hardware.
 Where the bytes physically live — your own NAS, a
 rented VPS, or a company's data center. This is the real trade-off
 axis, more than any feature list.
 Exit plan — can you get your photos and metadata
 back out in a standard format if you switch again later, or are
 you locked into one app's database?
 Quick picks
 Summary recommendations
 Use case 
 Pick 
 Why

 auto-backup, timeline, face grouping, and a fast-moving
 open-source project
 Best for families and shared albums 
 Noodle Gallery 
 Immich fork built specifically around multi-owner shared
 timelines, which upstream Immich only handles awkwardly
 Best encrypted cloud (no server needed) 
 Ente Photos 
 Zero-knowledge encryption with none of the setup work —
 closest thing to "just sign up" on this list
 Best free encrypted tier 
 Stingle Photos 
 End-to-end encrypted with a genuinely free 1GB tier and an
 F-Droid build
 Best if you already run Nextcloud 
 Nextcloud Memories 
 Adds a Google-Photos-style timeline and face recognition on
 top of storage you've already set up
 Best for low-power hardware 
 PiGallery2 
 Runs comfortably on a Raspberry Pi by staying read-only and
 directory-based instead of re-indexing everything
 Best face search on your own server 
 LibrePhotos 
 Machine-learning face clustering and semantic search without
 sending anything off your hardware
 The seven alternatives
 1 
 Immich
 The default answer, for good reason
 Immich is what most people mean when they say "self-hosted
 Google Photos." It's the tool that made self-hosted photo backup
 feel realistic instead of theoretical the mobile app backs up in
 the background exactly like Google's does, and once photos land
 on your server, Immich builds a timeline, groups faces, and lets
 you search by content ("dog," "birthday cake") using on-device
 machine learning models it runs itself. You'll notice the
 project is still moving fast: releases ship often, and the
 changelog reads like a team that actually uses their own
 software.
 Pros
 Mobile background backup that behaves like Google Photos,
 not an afterthought
 Face recognition and content search, computed locally on
 your server
 Active development with a large, responsive community
 No cloud dependency once it's running your data doesn't
 leave your network unless you choose to expose it
 Cons
 You need a server: a NAS, a mini PC, or a VPS, plus Docker
 Compose comfort
 Face recognition and thumbnail generation are
 CPU/GPU-hungry on large libraries a Raspberry Pi will
 struggle
 Still under 1.0 as a project; breaking changes between
 versions happen and upgrades need reading the release
 notes
 You're responsible for your own backups of the backup
 losing the server without an off-site copy means losing
 everything
 Migration notes: Immich has an official import
 tool for a Google Takeout export that maps albums and creation
 dates from the accompanying JSON files, so you don't lose that
 metadata the way you would with a plain drag-and-drop.
 Ideal for: Anyone with a home server (or
 willing to rent a small VPS) who wants the closest feature match
 to Google Photos, and doesn't mind occasional maintenance.
 Pricing: Free, self-hosted.
 Platforms: Docker (Linux/NAS/VPS), iOS,
 Android, web.
 Visit Immich 
 Directory entry 
 2 
 Noodle Gallery
 Immich's engine, rebuilt for sharing with other people
 Noodle Gallery is a community fork of Immich, and it's worth
 understanding what that actually means before dismissing it as
 "just Immich with extras." It rebases onto every upstream Immich
 release, so you get Immich's fixes and improvements
 automatically, while adding features built specifically around
 the one thing Immich itself is weakest at: multiple people
 contributing to the same photo library. Its "Shared Spaces" give
 each contributor a role (owner, editor, viewer), link photos by
 reference instead of duplicating storage, and merge face
 recognition across everyone's contributions without letting
 anyone see photos outside their permission. If you're the person
 a family keeps asking "can you just make one shared album for
 the trip," this is built for exactly that problem.
 Pros
 Genuine multi-owner albums with per-person roles, not just
 a read-only share link
 Global People search works across your library and every
 shared space you can access
 Native S3-compatible storage support (AWS S3, MinIO, R2,
 Backblaze B2) with a migration tool if you outgrow local
 disk
 Guided Google Takeout import wizard no command line
 required
 Database-compatible with Immich, so switching to or
 reverting from upstream Immich is a small config change,
 not a migration
 Cons
 Smaller community than upstream Immich, since it's a fork
 maintained by fewer people
 Being newer, it has had less real-world battle-testing at
 very large scale
 Inherits all of Immich's hardware requirements, plus a bit
 more for the sharing layer
 Worth knowing: the project is openly built with
 heavy AI-assisted development alongside human-led design and
 testing the maintainers are upfront about this rather than
 hiding it, which we'd rather see disclosed than discover later.
 Ideal for: Households or friend groups who've
 outgrown "everyone dumps photos in one shared Google album" and
 want real collaborative albums without a subscription.
 Pricing: Free and open-source (AGPL-3.0),
 self-hosted. Platforms: Docker, iOS, Android,
 web.
 Visit Noodle Gallery 
 Directory entry 
 3 
 Ente Photos
 For people who want privacy without running a server
 Not everyone wants to own a piece of hardware just to store
 photos, and that's a legitimate position self-hosting has real
 ongoing costs in time, not just money. Ente is what to pick
 instead. It's a hosted cloud service like Google Photos, but
 built on zero-knowledge, end-to-end encryption: your photos are
 encrypted on your device before they ever reach Ente's servers,
 and Ente's published architecture means the company itself
 cannot decrypt your library, even under legal compulsion. The
 apps look and feel close enough to Google Photos that
 non-technical family members won't need a tutorial.
 Pros
 Zero setup sign up and the mobile app backs up
 automatically, same as Google Photos
 End-to-end encryption means Ente can't view your photos
 even if it wanted to
 Open-source apps, so the encryption claims are
 independently verifiable rather than just marketing copy
 Family plan lets you share storage without sharing a
 single account
 Cons
 You're trusting a company with your storage bill, not
 yourself it's not free at meaningful capacity
 End-to-end encryption means Ente can't do server-side
 "magic" search on unencrypted content the way Google can;
 ML search runs on-device and is a lighter feature set
 Smaller company than Google, which cuts both ways: better
 incentives, but less certainty about long-term survival
 Ideal for: Anyone who wants real privacy
 guarantees but has no interest in owning a server or doing any
 maintenance.
 Pricing: Free tier with limited storage; paid
 plans scale by storage, with a family option.
 Platforms: iOS, Android, web, desktop
 (Windows/macOS/Linux).
 Visit Ente Photos 
 Directory entry 
 4 
 Stingle Photos
 Encrypted, and actually free at a small scale
 Stingle covers similar ground to Ente open-source, end-to-end
 encrypted backup with cross-device sync but positions itself
 differently: a genuinely usable free tier (1GB, pay only if you
 need more), no ads, and registration that asks for nothing but
 an email and password. It's built on Libsodium with XChaCha20
 and ECC, which is a reasonable, well-understood cryptographic
 foundation rather than something custom and unaudited. It's also
 on F-Droid, which matters if you specifically avoid Google Play
 on your phone.
 Pros
 1GB free tier with no forced upgrade nagging
 End-to-end encryption covers photos, videos, and their
 metadata, not just the file bytes
 Can capture photos/videos directly into the encrypted
 vault without unlocking the app first
 Available on F-Droid as well as Google Play and the App
 Store
 Cons
 Interface and feature depth (search, albums, editing) is
 noticeably more basic than Google Photos or Ente
 Smaller team and community than Ente or Immich, so support
 and update cadence are less predictable
 No meaningful AI search this is a vault-first tool, not a
 "browse by content" tool
 Ideal for: Someone who mainly wants a secure,
 private backup vault for sensitive photos rather than a full
 Google-Photos-style browsing experience.
 Pricing: 1GB free; paid tiers for more storage.
 Platforms: iOS, Android (Google Play and
 F-Droid).
 Visit Stingle Photos 
 Directory entry 
 5 
 Nextcloud Memories
 The obvious move if you already self-host storage
 If you're already running Nextcloud for file sync, this isn't
 really a new tool to evaluate it's the Memories app, which turns
 your existing Nextcloud instance into a Google-Photos-style
 timeline with face recognition, map view, and "on this day"
 memories, all sitting on storage you've already set up and
 already back up. Starting from scratch purely for photos, we'd
 point you to Immich first, since Immich's photo-specific tooling
 is more polished. But if Nextcloud is already your file layer,
 adding Memories is close to free no new server, no new backup
 routine, no new account to manage.
 Pros
 Zero additional infrastructure if Nextcloud is already
 your file storage
 Optional end-to-end encryption at the Nextcloud storage
 layer
 One login, one backup routine, one place your family
 already knows how to use
 Fully open-source and auditable codebase
 Cons
 Not worth setting up Nextcloud from scratch just for this
 it's a much bigger, more general system than a photo tool
 Face recognition and indexing performance depend heavily
 on your existing Nextcloud server's resources
 Photo-specific UX is noticeably less refined than Immich's
 purpose-built interface
 Ideal for: Existing Nextcloud users who want
 photo timeline and face search without adding a second
 self-hosted app to maintain.
 Pricing: Free, self-hosted (part of the
 Nextcloud ecosystem). Platforms: Docker/server
 install, iOS, Android, web.
 Visit Nextcloud 
 Directory entry 
 6 
 LibrePhotos
 Immich's older, search-focused sibling
 LibrePhotos predates Immich and takes a slightly different
 angle: rather than chasing mobile-backup polish, it leans into
 search face clustering, object and scene detection, and semantic
 search that lets you type something like "sunset over water" and
 get plausible results, all computed locally on your server via
 Django and machine learning models it runs itself. If your main
 frustration with leaving Google Photos is "but I actually use
 the search," this is worth a look specifically for that reason.
 The mobile experience is a React Native Android app rather than
 fully native iOS/Android apps, which is the clearest gap versus
 Immich.
 Pros
 Strong self-hosted face clustering and object/scene
 detection
 Semantic search that goes beyond simple filename or tag
 matching
 Handles RAW files and video, not just standard image
 formats
 Multi-user support, Docker/Kubernetes deployment options
 Cons
 No native iOS app Android only, via React Native
 Smaller, slower-moving community than Immich's
 Interface feels a generation behind Immich's, and setup
 documentation is thinner
 Ideal for: Self-hosters who prioritize search
 quality over mobile app polish, or who are specifically drawn to
 its ML-driven object detection.
 Pricing: Free, self-hosted, MIT licensed.
 Platforms: Docker, Kubernetes, web, Android.
 Visit LibrePhotos 
 Directory entry 
 7 
 PiGallery2
 For hardware too small to run the others
 Immich, Noodle Gallery, and LibrePhotos all lean on
 machine-learning indexing, which needs real CPU (or a GPU) to
 stay fast as your library grows. PiGallery2 takes the opposite
 approach on purpose: it's directory-first and read-only, meaning
 it displays whatever folder structure you already have instead
 of re-importing and re-organizing everything into its own
 database. That design is exactly why it runs comfortably on
 something as small as a Raspberry Pi there's far less happening
 under the hood. The trade-off is that you don't get face
 recognition or Google-Photos-style automatic organization; you
 get a fast, honest viewer for photos you've already organized
 yourself.
 Pros
 Genuinely lightweight — runs well on a Raspberry Pi or
 other low-power hardware
 Read-only by design, so it can never reorganize or damage
 your existing folder structure
 Fast setup: point it at a folder and it works
 Configurable user access control for shared households
 Cons
 No face recognition, no AI search, no automatic albums
 No native mobile backup app you still need another way to
 get phone photos onto the server first
 Best suited to people who already keep their photo folders
 organized, not as a replacement for Google Photos'
 automatic sorting
 Ideal for: Raspberry Pi or low-power NAS owners
 who want a fast photo viewer without the overhead of ML
 indexing, and who already manage their own folder structure.
 Pricing: Free, self-hosted, MIT licensed.
 Platforms: Docker (recommended), native
 Node.js.
 Visit PiGallery2 
 Directory entry 
 Getting your photos out of Google in the first place
 Whichever tool you pick, the move starts the same way: Google
 Takeout. Request an export of just Google Photos (skip the rest of
 your account data unless you need it too it slows the export down
 and bloats the download). Google splits large libraries into
 multiple zip files, and each photo ships with a matching
 .json sidecar file containing the original timestamp,
 GPS location, and album membership. That JSON file is the part
 people throw away by accident, and it's the part that lets a good
 import tool rebuild your timeline and albums correctly instead of
 dumping everything into one folder dated "today."
 Immich and Noodle Gallery both have import tooling built
 specifically to read those Takeout JSON sidecars, which is a real
 time-saver over a plain file copy. If you're moving to Ente or
 Stingle instead, expect a manual upload through their desktop apps,
 since neither is built around bulk Takeout imports the same way.
 Either way, don't delete anything from Google until you've verified
 the new library on a second device Takeout exports have been known
 to silently drop a handful of files on very large libraries, and you
 want to catch that before, not after, deleting the source.
 Honest drawbacks worth knowing before you switch
 Self-hosting means you are the backup admin. 
 Immich, Noodle Gallery, LibrePhotos, and PiGallery2 protect your
 privacy, not your data from hardware failure. If your server dies
 without an off-site copy, the photos are gone. Set up a second
 backup target before you trust any self-hosted tool with
 irreplaceable photos.
 Face recognition needs to relearn your faces. 
 None of these tools can import Google's face-tagging data, since
 Google doesn't export it in a usable form. Expect to re-tag faces
 once after migrating.
 Encrypted cloud tools trade some search power for
 privacy. 
 Ente and Stingle can't run the same server-side content analysis
 Google does on unencrypted photos, since they never have access to
 unencrypted photos. Their on-device search is good, but it's not a
 one-to-one replacement for "search any word and Google finds it."
 Mobile-only tools without a desktop app are inconvenient for
 large libraries. 
 If you're moving tens of thousands of photos at once, doing it
 from a phone app is slow. Prefer a tool with a desktop client or a
 bulk-import path for the initial migration.

 FAQ
 Can I keep Google Photos and just back up elsewhere too?
 Yes, and it's a reasonable middle step. Several tools here
 support automatic mobile backup the same way Google Photos

 Will I lose my face-tagging and search when I switch?
 Google Takeout does not export face-tag data in a form other
 tools can read, so you'll lose that layer and need to let the
 new tool re-scan your library. Album structure, captions, and
 timestamps do carry over if you use the JSON sidecar files
 correctly.
 Is self-hosting actually harder than it sounds? 
 It requires a server you control (a home NAS, a mini PC, or a
 rented VPS) and comfort with Docker Compose. It is not harder
 than setting up a home router, but it is more upfront work
 than downloading an app, and you are responsible for backups.

 Export first, preserve an untouched copy, then import and verify before deleting anything. Metadata can be distributed between image files, sidecar JSON files and album structures, so a successful file transfer is not proof that every date, location, album and video survived.
 Measure the library. Note the total size, approximate item count, oldest and newest dates, and the amount of video. Use those figures to choose a destination tier with room for growth.
 Request an original-quality export. Download a Google Takeout export that includes original files and metadata. Keep the downloaded archive unchanged as your first independent copy.
 Create a second copy. Copy the export to a separate disk or another storage location before importing. Do not use the destination service as the only copy during migration.
 Prepare the destination. Enable the account, install its desktop or mobile app, and confirm that the available capacity exceeds the export size. For Immich, finish server setup, user accounts, storage paths and backup jobs first.
 Import in batches. Ente documents a desktop workflow for importing a Google Takeout export. For other services, upload a small date range first so you can inspect how metadata and album folders are interpreted.
 Check dates and locations. Compare several old, recent and edited images against the original export. Verify capture time, timezone behavior, GPS data and orientation.
 Check albums and sharing. Confirm that representative albums contain the expected items. Shared links and family-library permissions usually must be recreated because they belong to the old service’s account system.
 Test videos and special formats. Play clips from different years, including long videos and motion-photo or Live Photo pairs if your library contains them. Look for missing audio, split still/video components or unsupported formats.
 Turn on automatic backup. After the historical import is sound, enable camera backup on each phone and set whether cellular data, background uploads and local deletion are allowed.
 Keep the old library temporarily. Leave Google Photos intact until the destination and your second copy pass spot checks. Deleting early removes your easiest recovery path.

 Missing albums: album membership is often represented by folder names or sidecar data rather than embedded in the image. Rebuild critical albums manually if the destination cannot map them.
 Videos that will not play: test codecs and container formats early. Retain the original file even if a destination creates a preview or converted copy.

 Pick iCloud Photos for an Apple-heavy household and OneDrive when Microsoft 365 already covers your storage needs. Ecosystem integration reduces friction for automatic backup and family sharing, but it also ties your library to that account platform.

A self-hosted server needs the same arrangement; RAID or mirrored disks improve availability but do not replace a separate backup.

 Leave room for several years of phone photos and videos, plus thumbnails and edited copies created by the destination. A tier that exactly matches today’s export can block uploads sooner than expected.

 With Google Photos ending free unlimited storage and iCloud costs scaling with library size, a NAS is increasingly the best way to keep full-resolution photos without monthly fees.
 A personal NAS gives you a Google Photos experience you actually own. Automatic mobile backup, face recognition, shared family albums, and a timeline interface are all available — without a subscription and without your photos sitting on someone else's servers. The best NAS photo apps in 2026 have closed much of the gap with Google Photos and iCloud, and in some ways — particularly privacy and storage economics — they have surpassed them.
 Choosing the right NAS for photos comes down to software quality, CPU performance for AI indexing, network speed for large photo imports, and how well the mobile sync app works day to day. Synology Photos remains the gold standard for ease of use, while Immich has emerged as a powerful self-hosted alternative for users comfortable with a more hands-on setup.

 Synology Photos vs Google Photos: What You Get and What You Lose
 Synology Photos is the most polished NAS photo application available in 2026. It provides a familiar chronological timeline, automatic organization by date and location, shared family albums, and face recognition that runs entirely on your NAS hardware. It is available as a free package on any Synology NAS and works with both the Synology Photos mobile app and any web browser.
 Compared to Google Photos, Synology Photos matches the core experience well: backup all your photos automatically, browse by date, search by face or location, and share albums with family members. What you give up is Google's AI search quality — Google's "find photos of me at the beach in 2022" natural language search is genuinely impressive, and Synology Photos is not quite there yet, though it is improving. You also lose Google's automatic video stabilization, magic eraser, and on-device suggestions that Google Photos shows in your camera roll.
 What you gain is significant: unlimited storage (limited only by your drives, not a subscription tier), full-resolution originals always, no monthly fee, and your data never leaving your premises. For families paying for multiple iCloud or Google One plans, the NAS pays for itself in two to three years of avoided subscription costs.
 Mobile backup behavior is important to understand. Synology Photos on iOS backs up photos when the app is open or in the background with background app refresh enabled. Unlike Google Photos which runs silently and aggressively in the background, you may occasionally find a week's worth of photos waiting to sync when you open the Synology Photos app. On Android, background sync is somewhat more reliable. Most users find this acceptable; it becomes an issue only if you are counting on having photos backed up immediately after taking them.
 Setting Up Mobile Photo Sync to Your NAS
 For Synology NAS, the Synology Photos app (iOS and Android) is the recommended path. It handles automatic backup of your camera roll, creates albums, lets you browse your entire library, and supports shared albums with family members who each have their own NAS user account. Setup takes about ten minutes: install the Synology Photos package on the NAS, create user accounts, and log in on each phone.
 For QNAP, QuMagie handles mobile sync with a similar feature set. The mobile client is solid for Android; iOS users sometimes report a slightly rougher experience with background sync.
 Immich — available on TerraMaster, UGREEN, and any Docker-capable NAS — has excellent iOS and Android apps that behave more like Google Photos in terms of background sync aggressiveness. Immich's mobile clients run continuous background uploads reliably on both platforms, which gives it an edge over Synology Photos for users who want set-it-and-forget-it sync behavior. The tradeoff is that Immich requires manual setup via Docker Compose or a container manager, and updates are more hands-on than a DSM package.
 AI Photo Indexing: Face Recognition, Object Search, and Location Tags
 Synology Photos runs face detection and recognition on the NAS itself using a neural network model included with DSM. It progressively scans your library after import, grouping detected faces into clusters that you can label with names. Once labeled, it can find photos of that person across your entire library. The process takes time for large libraries — a library of 50,000 photos can take several days to fully index on a DS224+ — but it runs in the background without interrupting normal use.
 Object recognition in Synology Photos allows searching for terms like "dog," "car," "beach," or "food" and returns matching photos. Location indexing pulls GPS EXIF data from photos and organizes them on a map. This is particularly useful for travel libraries.
 QNAP's QuMagie uses a similar on-device AI approach with competitive face and scene recognition. Immich's machine learning stack is open-source and actively developed — its face recognition and CLIP-based semantic search (which allows natural language queries) have improved dramatically in recent versions.
 The privacy advantage of on-device AI indexing is significant: your photos are never sent to a third-party server for analysis. This matters particularly for family photos and for users in jurisdictions with strong privacy laws or personal privacy preferences.
 RAW Files and Video: Storage Planning for Serious Photographers
 Smartphone photos average 3–8 MB each in JPEG or HEIC format. That sounds manageable until you realize a family of four shooting 10,000 photos per year generates 30–80 GB annually in phone photos alone. Add video and you can easily hit 200–500 GB per year from smartphones.
 Serious photographers with DSLR or mirrorless cameras face a much larger storage challenge. RAW files from modern cameras range from 20 MB for entry-level APS-C cameras to 90 MB for high-megapixel full-frame sensors (Sony A7RV, Nikon Z8). A single shooting day producing 1,000 RAW files can generate 30–90 GB of data. Photographers who shoot both RAW and JPEG doubles the storage requirement.
 For photographers with large RAW libraries, 2.5G Ethernet makes a real difference during import. Copying 50 GB of RAW files over gigabit Ethernet takes around seven minutes at 100 MB/s; over 2.5G it drops to under three minutes at 250 MB/s. This is why the QNAP TS-264 with dual 2.5G ports is particularly appealing for photographers — faster imports mean less time waiting and more time editing.
 For storage sizing, a reasonable starting point is 2 TB for smartphone-only families, 4–8 TB for mixed smartphone and entry-level camera users, and 8–20+ TB for working photographers or serious amateurs with years of RAW archives. Always leave 20% headroom on your volume and plan your RAID strategy accordingly: RAID 1 (mirroring) on a 2-bay gives you one drive's worth of usable space; RAID 5 on a 4-bay gives you three drives' worth.
 Remote Access for Family Photo Sharing
 Synology Photos handles family sharing through shared albums and personal spaces. Each family member gets their own NAS user account with their own Personal Space (visible only to them) alongside a Shared Space that the whole family can see. Photo albums can be shared with specific users or via a public link with optional password protection.
 For remote access, Synology QuickConnect is the easiest option — it creates a relay connection through Synology's servers so you can access your NAS from anywhere without port forwarding or a static IP. Performance is adequate for browsing photos but is relay-based, meaning it is slower than a direct connection. For better remote performance, configure DDNS (dynamic DNS) with port forwarding, or use the NAS's built-in VPN server so remote devices connect directly to your home network.
 Immich handles remote sharing through a link-based approach: you can share individual photos or albums via a shareable link, with optional expiration and password. Remote access for the owner is typically done through a reverse proxy or VPN — Nginx Proxy Manager running as a Docker container on the same NAS is a popular approach.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I replace Google Photos with a NAS?
 Yes, with Synology Photos or Immich you can replicate most of what Google Photos does — automatic mobile backup, face recognition, shared albums, and a timeline view. You lose Google's search quality and on-device suggestions, but you gain full control over your data with no storage fees and no subscription required.
 Does Synology Photos do face recognition?
 Yes. Synology Photos includes face recognition that runs entirely on the NAS — your photos are never sent to the cloud for analysis. The NAS indexes faces locally and groups photos by person. Recognition accuracy improves as you confirm and label faces over time.
 How much storage do I need for a photo library?
 A library of 100,000 JPEGs from a smartphone averages 300–500 GB depending on camera quality. RAW files from DSLR or mirrorless cameras are 5–10x larger per photo — a 30-megapixel RAW file is typically 25–40 MB. Serious photographers with large RAW libraries should plan for 4–20 TB or more.
 Can I access my NAS photos from my phone when away from home?
 Yes. Synology QuickConnect lets you access Synology Photos from anywhere without configuring port forwarding. DDNS is another option. For the most secure remote access, set up a VPN on the NAS so your phone connects to your home network before accessing photos.

 Best apps for organizing a NAS photo library in 2026
 Moving thirty thousand photos to a NAS is easy. Making them findable is the hard part. These eight desktop tools handle indexing, dedup, and face recognition on your own hardware.

 Why photos on a NAS need a real organizer
 Moving a photo library off Google Photos or iCloud onto your own NAS is the easy half. Then you open the share and stare at a decade of folders titled 2019-04 , IMG_20200812_190232.jpg , and duplicate_backup_final_v2 . XDA’s writer put it well after making the same move: the NAS taught them a lot about how they actually think about their memories, and the takeaway was that storage is not organization. You need an app on top that indexes, deduplicates, tags, and lets you search by face or place.
 We loaded the same 47,000-photo test library onto a Synology DS923+ over NFS and pointed each of these eight desktop and self-hosted tools at it. The rankings are based on first-index time, disk overhead, dedup accuracy, and how long it took to answer “show me every photo with my niece from summer 2021” without cheating.
 What to look for in a photo library organizer
 Non-destructive indexing. The originals stay where you put them. The organizer builds a database next to them.
 Fast face and object recognition. A good model finds people across a decade, including baby-to-teenager transitions.
 Search that actually works. Filter by date, geotag, camera, aperture, person, keyword, all combinable.
 Deduplication with a real preview. Similar photos (bracketed exposures, near-duplicates) should show side by side before deletion.
 Sidecar-based metadata. Ratings, keywords, and edits stored in XMP sidecars so switching apps later is not a data-loss event.
 A companion mobile app. Half the value of a self-hosted library is being able to browse it from a phone on the couch.

 The eight photo apps we would trust with a family archive
 1. Immich, the Google-Photos-shaped app that finally feels finished
 Immich is the self-hosted photo library that closed the “but the mobile app is not good enough” gap. Its Android and iOS clients auto-upload, its web UI groups by day and month like Google Photos, and its face-recognition model is fast enough on a modest x86 server that the first pass of a 40,000-photo library completes overnight.
 Where it falls short: Ships fast, which sometimes means a schema migration between releases. Watch the release notes; back up the database before major bumps.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Fully open-source
 Paid: None
 vs Google Photos: You own the data and the search index
 Runs on: Docker on Windows, macOS, or Linux hosts, plus your NAS.
 Download: immich.app 
 Bottom line: Our current top pick for a family photo library moving off a cloud provider.
 2. PhotoPrism, the deep-search classic
 PhotoPrism predates Immich and remains the strongest option for search-heavy libraries. Its TensorFlow-based classifier tags photos with hundreds of labels (beach, cake, snow, cathedral), and its search grammar lets you combine face, tag, place, and camera in one query.
 Where it falls short: Some advanced features (bulk edits, private albums) sit behind a “Pro” purchase. Interface is more classical than Immich’s.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Community edition
 Paid: One-time Pro key
 vs Immich: Better search grammar, slower to feel modern
 Runs on: Docker on any host, ARM64 supported.
 Download: photoprism.app 
 Bottom line: The one to pick if searching a decade of vacation photos matters more than a phone-shaped upload experience.
 3. digiKam, the desktop cataloger that respects your metadata
 digiKam is a native desktop app (KDE roots, runs on all three OSes) that reads and writes proper XMP sidecars, so every rating, keyword, and adjustment travels with the file. It does not need a running server; it holds its database next to the library and stays out of the way.
 Where it falls short: Not a client-server app. There is no first-party mobile companion; you browse on the desktop.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Full application
 Paid: None
 vs Lightroom Classic: Similar cataloging depth, no subscription
 Runs on: Windows, macOS, Linux.
 Download: digikam.org 
 Bottom line: The pick for photographers who want a real desktop cataloger and sidecar-portable metadata.
 4. Adobe Bridge, the free Adobe surface many people forget exists
 Adobe Bridge is Adobe’s free asset browser and hands off cleanly to Lightroom Classic, Photoshop, and Camera Raw. If your library is on a NAS and you already pay for Creative Cloud, Bridge lets you rate, keyword, and batch-rename thousands of photos without importing them into Lightroom Classic.
 Where it falls short: Adobe ID required. Being free depends on Adobe keeping it that way (it has been free for years, but the future is theirs).
 Pricing: 
 Free: With an Adobe ID
 Paid: Bundled with Creative Cloud subscriptions
 vs Lightroom Classic: Lighter, no destructive edits, no catalog headaches
 Runs on: Windows, macOS.
 Download: adobe.com/products/bridge 
 Bottom line: If you already use Adobe tools, Bridge is the fastest way to catalog a NAS library into Lightroom Classic later.
 5. Excire Foto, the offline auto-tagger that impresses
 Excire Foto runs a local AI model that keywords a library without a cloud round-trip. Point it at a NAS share, walk away for a few hours, come back to keywords like “beach,” “sunset,” “toddler,” “dog” applied across the archive. Search then works on those keywords immediately.
 Where it falls short: Paid product, and the buy-once model still means paying to move up major versions.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Trial
 Paid: A one-time perpetual license per major version
 vs cloud AI keywording: Runs on your machine; nothing leaves the network
 Runs on: Windows, macOS.
 Download: excire.com 
 Bottom line: The right pick if you specifically care about high-quality automatic keywording and refuse cloud services.
 6. Mylio Photos, the peer-to-peer sync that skips the server
 Mylio Photos takes a different approach: no server, no cloud. Devices you sign into (laptop, phone, iPad, NAS as a “vault”) sync photos directly when they see each other on the network. The library on the NAS is the master; each device pulls the resolution it needs.
 Where it falls short: The free tier caps devices and features. Adding a lot of viewer devices pushes you into the paid plan.
 Pricing: 
 Free: A limited number of devices
 Paid: Mylio+ subscription
 vs Immich: No server to run; every device has to be online occasionally to sync
 Runs on: Windows, macOS, plus iOS and Android for viewing.
 Download: mylio.com 
 Bottom line: The right pick for readers allergic to running any container and comfortable with a subscription for viewers.
 7. XnView MP, the lightweight batch-processing browser
 XnView MP is a file browser for images: pick a folder, see thumbnails of every file, batch-rename, batch-convert, edit EXIF, apply keywords, and export contact sheets. It reads more image formats than most competitors combined, which matters for an archive that has HEIC, RAW, TIFF, PSD, and older camera formats mixed together.
 Where it falls short: Not a modern face-recognition app; it is a browser and batch tool.
 Pricing: 
 Free: For personal use
 Paid: Business license
 vs digiKam: Faster to use for one-off batch tasks; less structured cataloging
 Runs on: Windows, macOS, Linux.
 Download: xnview.com 
 Bottom line: The tool to reach for when the task is “rename 6,000 files to a sensible pattern” rather than “index my entire library.”
 8. Nextcloud Memories, the Photos add-on for the Nextcloud crowd
 Nextcloud Memories is a Photos-style app that sits on top of an existing Nextcloud install. It reads the photos that are already on your Nextcloud share, applies face and object recognition, and gives you a Google-Photos-shaped view without moving anything.
 Where it falls short: You have to already run Nextcloud, which adds its own set of moving parts.
 Pricing: 
 Free: Open-source add-on
 Paid: Nextcloud Enterprise, only for larger deployments
 vs Immich: A better fit if your files already live in Nextcloud
 Runs on: Any Nextcloud host.
 Download: Nextcloud Memories on GitHub 
 Bottom line: The right pick when Nextcloud is already the center of your self-hosted life.
 How to pick the right organizer
 If you want a Google Photos replacement with a real mobile app: Immich.
 If your library is huge and search matters more than upload: PhotoPrism.
 If you are a photographer with a proper metadata workflow: digiKam or Adobe Bridge into Lightroom Classic.
 If cloud services are not welcome on your network: Excire Foto for keywording, digiKam for cataloging.

 The initial indexing pass is memory-hungry (a few gigabytes for face and object recognition), then daily use drops to hundreds of megabytes. A small mini PC with 8GB is comfortable; a NAS with 4GB will work but slow the first pass.

 digiKam, XnView MP, and PhotoPrism can. Immich flags near-duplicates in recent releases. For aggressive dedup, dupeGuru Picture Edition is a common companion tool.

 No. Immich, PhotoPrism, digiKam, XnView MP, Excire Foto, and Nextcloud Memories all run entirely on your network. Mylio Photos uses your local network for sync and only reaches the internet if you enable optional cloud backup.

 With Google Photos ending free unlimited storage and iCloud costs scaling with library size, a NAS is increasingly the best way to keep full-resolution photos without monthly fees.
 A personal NAS gives you a Google Photos experience you actually own. Automatic mobile backup, face recognition, shared family albums, and a timeline interface are all available — without a subscription and without your photos sitting on someone else's servers. The best NAS photo apps in 2026 have closed much of the gap with Google Photos and iCloud, and in some ways — particularly privacy and storage economics — they have surpassed them.
 Choosing the right NAS for photos comes down to software quality, CPU performance for AI indexing, network speed for large photo imports, and how well the mobile sync app works day to day. Synology Photos remains the gold standard for ease of use, while Immich has emerged as a powerful self-hosted alternative for users comfortable with a more hands-on setup.

 Synology Photos vs Google Photos: What You Get and What You Lose
 Synology Photos is the most polished NAS photo application available in 2026. It provides a familiar chronological timeline, automatic organization by date and location, shared family albums, and face recognition that runs entirely on your NAS hardware. It is available as a free package on any Synology NAS and works with both the Synology Photos mobile app and any web browser.
 Compared to Google Photos, Synology Photos matches the core experience well: backup all your photos automatically, browse by date, search by face or location, and share albums with family members. What you give up is Google's AI search quality — Google's "find photos of me at the beach in 2022" natural language search is genuinely impressive, and Synology Photos is not quite there yet, though it is improving. You also lose Google's automatic video stabilization, magic eraser, and on-device suggestions that Google Photos shows in your camera roll.
 What you gain is significant: unlimited storage (limited only by your drives, not a subscription tier), full-resolution originals always, no monthly fee, and your data never leaving your premises. For families paying for multiple iCloud or Google One plans, the NAS pays for itself in two to three years of avoided subscription costs.
 Mobile backup behavior is important to understand. Synology Photos on iOS backs up photos when the app is open or in the background with background app refresh enabled. Unlike Google Photos which runs silently and aggressively in the background, you may occasionally find a week's worth of photos waiting to sync when you open the Synology Photos app. On Android, background sync is somewhat more reliable. Most users find this acceptable; it becomes an issue only if you are counting on having photos backed up immediately after taking them.
 Setting Up Mobile Photo Sync to Your NAS
 For Synology NAS, the Synology Photos app (iOS and Android) is the recommended path. It handles automatic backup of your camera roll, creates albums, lets you browse your entire library, and supports shared albums with family members who each have their own NAS user account. Setup takes about ten minutes: install the Synology Photos package on the NAS, create user accounts, and log in on each phone.
 For QNAP, QuMagie handles mobile sync with a similar feature set. The mobile client is solid for Android; iOS users sometimes report a slightly rougher experience with background sync.
 Immich — available on TerraMaster, UGREEN, and any Docker-capable NAS — has excellent iOS and Android apps that behave more like Google Photos in terms of background sync aggressiveness. Immich's mobile clients run continuous background uploads reliably on both platforms, which gives it an edge over Synology Photos for users who want set-it-and-forget-it sync behavior. The tradeoff is that Immich requires manual setup via Docker Compose or a container manager, and updates are more hands-on than a DSM package.
 AI Photo Indexing: Face Recognition, Object Search, and Location Tags
 Synology Photos runs face detection and recognition on the NAS itself using a neural network model included with DSM. It progressively scans your library after import, grouping detected faces into clusters that you can label with names. Once labeled, it can find photos of that person across your entire library. The process takes time for large libraries — a library of 50,000 photos can take several days to fully index on a DS224+ — but it runs in the background without interrupting normal use.
 Object recognition in Synology Photos allows searching for terms like "dog," "car," "beach," or "food" and returns matching photos. Location indexing pulls GPS EXIF data from photos and organizes them on a map. This is particularly useful for travel libraries.
 QNAP's QuMagie uses a similar on-device AI approach with competitive face and scene recognition. Immich's machine learning stack is open-source and actively developed — its face recognition and CLIP-based semantic search (which allows natural language queries) have improved dramatically in recent versions.
 The privacy advantage of on-device AI indexing is significant: your photos are never sent to a third-party server for analysis. This matters particularly for family photos and for users in jurisdictions with strong privacy laws or personal privacy preferences.
 RAW Files and Video: Storage Planning for Serious Photographers
 Smartphone photos average 3–8 MB each in JPEG or HEIC format. That sounds manageable until you realize a family of four shooting 10,000 photos per year generates 30–80 GB annually in phone photos alone. Add video and you can easily hit 200–500 GB per year from smartphones.
 Serious photographers with DSLR or mirrorless cameras face a much larger storage challenge. RAW files from modern cameras range from 20 MB for entry-level APS-C cameras to 90 MB for high-megapixel full-frame sensors (Sony A7RV, Nikon Z8). A single shooting day producing 1,000 RAW files can generate 30–90 GB of data. Photographers who shoot both RAW and JPEG doubles the storage requirement.
 For photographers with large RAW libraries, 2.5G Ethernet makes a real difference during import. Copying 50 GB of RAW files over gigabit Ethernet takes around seven minutes at 100 MB/s; over 2.5G it drops to under three minutes at 250 MB/s. This is why the QNAP TS-264 with dual 2.5G ports is particularly appealing for photographers — faster imports mean less time waiting and more time editing.
 For storage sizing, a reasonable starting point is 2 TB for smartphone-only families, 4–8 TB for mixed smartphone and entry-level camera users, and 8–20+ TB for working photographers or serious amateurs with years of RAW archives. Always leave 20% headroom on your volume and plan your RAID strategy accordingly: RAID 1 (mirroring) on a 2-bay gives you one drive's worth of usable space; RAID 5 on a 4-bay gives you three drives' worth.
 Remote Access for Family Photo Sharing
 Synology Photos handles family sharing through shared albums and personal spaces. Each family member gets their own NAS user account with their own Personal Space (visible only to them) alongside a Shared Space that the whole family can see. Photo albums can be shared with specific users or via a public link with optional password protection.
 For remote access, Synology QuickConnect is the easiest option — it creates a relay connection through Synology's servers so you can access your NAS from anywhere without port forwarding or a static IP. Performance is adequate for browsing photos but is relay-based, meaning it is slower than a direct connection. For better remote performance, configure DDNS (dynamic DNS) with port forwarding, or use the NAS's built-in VPN server so remote devices connect directly to your home network.
 Immich handles remote sharing through a link-based approach: you can share individual photos or albums via a shareable link, with optional expiration and password. Remote access for the owner is typically done through a reverse proxy or VPN — Nginx Proxy Manager running as a Docker container on the same NAS is a popular approach.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 Can I replace Google Photos with a NAS?
 Yes, with Synology Photos or Immich you can replicate most of what Google Photos does — automatic mobile backup, face recognition, shared albums, and a timeline view. You lose Google's search quality and on-device suggestions, but you gain full control over your data with no storage fees and no subscription required.
 Does Synology Photos do face recognition?
 Yes. Synology Photos includes face recognition that runs entirely on the NAS — your photos are never sent to the cloud for analysis. The NAS indexes faces locally and groups photos by person. Recognition accuracy improves as you confirm and label faces over time.
 How much storage do I need for a photo library?
 A library of 100,000 JPEGs from a smartphone averages 300–500 GB depending on camera quality. RAW files from DSLR or mirrorless cameras are 5–10x larger per photo — a 30-megapixel RAW file is typically 25–40 MB. Serious photographers with large RAW libraries should plan for 4–20 TB or more.
 Can I access my NAS photos from my phone when away from home?
 Yes. Synology QuickConnect lets you access Synology Photos from anywhere without configuring port forwarding. DDNS is another option. For the most secure remote access, set up a VPN on the NAS so your phone connects to your home network before accessing photos.

 What Google Photos does
 Google Photos is Google’s service for backing up, organizing and sharing photos and videos, with apps for Android and iOS and a web version. It backs up the camera roll automatically in Original quality or in Storage saver, which compresses photos to 16 MP and videos to 1080p. Machine learning groups faces of people and pets, stacks similar shots, collects documents and screenshots into albums and builds memories, and search accepts natural-language queries. Photos and albums can be shared with anyone, including people without the app, and partner sharing gives a trusted contact access to your library. The whole library can be exported through Google Takeout.
 Why people look for an alternative
 Storage counts against a shared quota. Since 1 June 2021, new uploads in Storage saver count toward the free 15 GB that Gmail, Drive and Photos share. Only items uploaded before that date, and those from Pixel 1 to 5 phones, are exempt. More space needs a paid Google One plan.
 Running out of space affects the whole account. When you are over quota, new photos stop backing up. Google says that if an account stays over quota for 2 years or more, all of its content may be removed, including Gmail and Drive.
 Inactivity. Google’s help pages warn that content may be deleted if you are inactive in Google Photos for 2 years or more.
 Data held by Google. Google says Photos content is not used for advertising, but users can choose to make Photos data available to other Google services that do support ads. Google does not say the library is end-to-end encrypted.
 Exports need reassembling. Takeout puts metadata such as dates and locations in separate JSON files, and importers have to match these back to each photo. PhotoPrism and Ente both document this step.
 What to compare in an alternative
 Automatic phone backup. An official mobile app that uploads in the background, or reliance on a third-party sync app.
 Where the data lives and who can read it. Your own server, the developers’ cloud, and whether the library is encrypted end to end.
 Search and organization. Face recognition, semantic search, maps and memories, and whether the machine learning runs on your server, on your devices or through an outside service.
 Sharing. Shared albums, public links, partner sharing and accounts for family members.
 Takeout import. Whether the importer reads the JSON metadata (dates, locations, descriptions) and recreates albums.
 Cost of running it. RAM and CPU for machine learning, disk space for the originals, and a separate backup of the server itself.
 Which one to choose
 Immich comes closest to the Google Photos experience. It has native Android and iOS apps with background backup, a timeline, face grouping, smart search and partner sharing. It needs at least 6 GB of RAM; Takeout imports go through the community tool immich-go. Ente Photos is the choice if you care most about privacy: everything is encrypted end to end and machine learning runs on your devices. You can use its hosted service, which has a free tier, or self-host the server, and its desktop app imports Takeout archives. If you already run Nextcloud, Memories adds a fast timeline, maps and face tagging (through Nextcloud’s Recognize or Face Recognition apps), and the Nextcloud apps handle phone upload. PhotoPrism is a strong fit for browsing and searching a large existing archive and reads Takeout metadata, but phone backup depends on a third-party WebDAV app, and some features need a paid membership.

 The Full Ranking
 1. Immich — Best Overall
 Immich is the best self-hosted photo management app for most people. It is the closest thing to a self-hosted Google Photos that exists. Native iOS and Android apps with automatic background upload, CLIP-based smart search (search “dog on beach” and it works), facial recognition with person grouping, a map view, shared albums, partner sharing, and a fast, polished web UI. With 90,000+ GitHub stars, it is one of the most popular self-hosted projects on the internet.
 Immich runs four containers: the main server, a machine learning service, PostgreSQL with pgvecto.rs, and Valkey (Redis-compatible cache). It needs 4 GB of RAM minimum and 8 GB if you want responsive ML processing. The setup is straightforward with Docker Compose and an .env file.
 Pros: 
 Native mobile apps with auto-upload (iOS and Android)
 CLIP smart search — describe what you want in natural language
 Facial recognition with person grouping
 Map view with GPS data
 Shared albums and partner sharing
 Timeline view identical to Google Photos
 External library support (scan existing folders)
 Very active development — weekly releases
 90,000+ GitHub stars, massive community
 Cons: 
 Under active development — breaking changes between versions
 Higher resource usage (4–8 GB RAM with ML)
 No RAW file support in the web viewer (thumbnails work)
 No plugin system
 Requires PostgreSQL with vector extensions (not a generic Postgres)
 Best for: Anyone replacing Google Photos, iCloud Photos, or Amazon Photos. Families, individuals, anyone who wants mobile auto-upload with smart search.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Immich 
 2. PhotoPrism — Best for AI Features
 PhotoPrism is the most mature AI-powered photo management app in the self-hosted space. It indexes your existing library and applies TensorFlow-based classification, facial recognition, location mapping, and color analysis. Excellent RAW file support (including DNG, CR2, ARW), live photo playback, panorama viewing, and automatic album creation by subject, location, and date.
 PhotoPrism is written in Go and uses MariaDB for its database. It needs 4 GB of RAM minimum and 4 GB of swap for indexing large libraries. The Essentials edition is free for personal use; the Plus edition adds advanced features for sponsors.
 Pros: 
 Mature AI classification and tagging
 Excellent RAW file support
 Automatic albums (by subject, place, date, camera)
 Live photo and panorama support
 Face recognition with clustering
 WebDAV access for direct file management
 Stable, well-tested codebase
 Good documentation
 Cons: 
 No mobile app with auto-upload (web-only, or use third-party sync)
 Some advanced features require sponsorship (Plus edition)
 Slower indexing on large libraries than Immich
 Higher disk usage from thumbnail generation (~50% of library size)
 Written in Go — harder to contribute to than Python/JS projects
 Best for: Photographers with large existing libraries who want AI tagging, RAW support, and a stable platform. Users who don’t need mobile auto-upload.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host PhotoPrism 
 3. LibrePhotos — Best Fully Free Option
 LibrePhotos is a fully open-source (MIT license) photo management app with face recognition, auto-tagging, location browsing, and timeline views. It is a fork of the discontinued OwnPhotos project, built with Django on the backend and React on the frontend. Every feature is free — there is no paid tier.
 LibrePhotos runs four containers: a Django backend, a React frontend, PostgreSQL, and Nginx. It requires 4 GB of RAM minimum and 8 GB for comfortable face recognition processing.
 Pros: 
 Fully free and open source (MIT license)
 Face recognition and grouping
 Auto-tagging with object detection
 Location-based browsing with map view
 Timeline view
 No paid tier — everything is included
 Multi-user support
 Cons: 
 Slower development pace than Immich or PhotoPrism
 No native mobile app (web only)
 No mobile auto-upload
 Indexing is slow on large libraries
 Smaller community (~7K GitHub stars)
 UI is less polished than Immich or PhotoPrism
 Documentation is sparse in places
 Best for: Users who want a fully FOSS photo management solution with face recognition and don’t need mobile auto-upload or cutting-edge AI features.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host LibrePhotos 
 4. Lychee — Best for Photographers
 Lychee is a self-hosted photo management app focused on gallery presentation and sharing rather than AI-powered library management. It excels at organizing albums, presenting photos with a clean minimal UI, generating public sharing links, and displaying EXIF metadata. Lychee v7 runs on FrankenPHP with Laravel Octane for fast performance.
 Lychee needs just 2 GB of RAM and runs three containers (app, MariaDB, optional Redis). It is the best option for anyone who wants to present and share curated collections rather than manage a personal photo dump.
 Pros: 
 Beautiful, minimal gallery UI
 Public sharing with custom URLs
 Album-based organization
 EXIF data display
 Multi-user with permissions
 Lightweight (2 GB RAM)
 Smart albums (by tag, date, star rating)
 Import from Flickr, URL, or filesystem
 Cons: 
 No face recognition or AI features
 No mobile app
 No auto-upload from phone
 No map view
 Not designed for massive personal libraries
 No video management features
 Best for: Photographers sharing portfolios, event photography galleries, curated collections meant for viewing. Not for personal photo library management.
 Read our full guide: How to Self-Host Lychee 
 5. Photoview — Best Lightweight Gallery
 Photoview is a lightweight, read-only photo gallery that scans existing folders on your filesystem and presents them through a clean web UI. It generates thumbnails, detects faces, reads EXIF data for map views, and supports multi-user access with per-user media directories. It never moves or modifies your original files.
 Photoview needs just 1 GB of RAM (2 GB recommended for face detection) and runs two containers (the app and MariaDB). It is the simplest option on this list — point it at your existing photo directories and browse.
 Pros: 
 Extremely lightweight (1 GB RAM)
 Scans existing folder structure — no import needed
 Never modifies original files
 Basic face detection

 Fast thumbnail generation
 Simple setup
 Cons: 
 Read-only — cannot upload, edit, or organize through the UI
 No mobile app
 No smart search or AI tagging
 No sharing features
 No album creation (follows folder structure only)
 Smaller community, slower development
 Limited video support
 Best for: Users who already have photos organized in folders on a NAS or server and want a fast gallery viewer without moving files. Ideal companion to Syncthing or Nextcloud file sync.

 6. Piwigo — Best for Large Collections
 Piwigo is the veteran of self-hosted photo management with over 23 years of active development (since 2002). It is a gallery and organization tool built for managing and sharing large photo collections. With 350+ plugins, batch operations, granular user permissions, and proven scalability to 500,000+ photos, Piwigo is the enterprise-grade option.
 Piwigo needs just 1 GB of RAM and runs two containers (the LinuxServer.io image and MariaDB). It is rock-solid and well-understood, but it is a traditional photo gallery — no AI features, no mobile auto-upload, no face recognition.
 Pros: 
 23 years of development — extremely mature and stable

 Cons: 
 No AI features (no face recognition, no smart search)
 No mobile app with auto-upload

 Plugin quality varies (community-maintained)
 PHP-based — some performance limitations at extreme scale
 No map view without plugins
 Best for: Organizations, photography clubs, or large family archives that need proven reliability, fine-grained access control, and plugin extensibility. Not a Google Photos replacement.

 How We Evaluated
 We ranked each app on six criteria:
 Google Photos parity — How close does it come to replacing Google Photos? Mobile app, auto-upload, smart search, and face recognition are the table stakes.
 Setup and maintenance — How many containers, how much RAM, how complex is the initial configuration? Self-hosting should not require a weekend of debugging.
 Feature depth — AI capabilities, sharing options, multi-user support, external library scanning, video handling.
 Resource efficiency — RAM, CPU, and disk requirements matter when you are running multiple services on one server.
 Community and longevity — GitHub activity, documentation quality, community size, release cadence. A dead project is worse than a limited one.
 Use case fit — Not everyone needs a Google Photos clone. Photographers, families, organizations, and minimalists have different needs. We reward apps that serve their target audience well.
 Immich wins because it is the only self-hosted app that genuinely competes with Google Photos on the dimensions that matter most: mobile auto-upload, smart search, and a polished daily-use experience. PhotoPrism is the best alternative for users who prioritize AI maturity and RAW support over mobile convenience.
 Frequently Asked Questions
 How much storage do I need for a self-hosted photo library?
 Plan for your raw library size plus 30-50% overhead for thumbnails, ML embeddings, and video transcodes. A 500 GB photo library typically needs 650-750 GB total. Use a local SSD for the database and ML cache, and a larger HDD or NAS mount for the actual media files. All tools on this list support external storage mounts.
 Can I import my existing Google Photos library?
 Yes. Use Google Takeout to export your photos, then import into Immich (CLI bulk upload or External Libraries), PhotoPrism (originals folder scan), or LibrePhotos (scan directories). Immich and PhotoPrism both preserve EXIF metadata including dates and GPS coordinates during import.
 Do I need a GPU for photo management?
 No, but it helps. Face recognition and smart search run on CPU by default in all tools listed here. An NVIDIA GPU or Intel iGPU accelerates ML processing significantly — reducing initial library scan time from days to hours for large libraries. Immich and PhotoPrism both support NVIDIA CUDA and Intel OpenVINO acceleration.
 Which app is best for families?
 Immich. It has the best mobile app (iOS and Android auto-upload), partner sharing (grant full library access to a family member), shared albums, and per-user storage isolation. The mobile experience is closest to Google Photos, which makes adoption easy for non-technical family members.
 Can I run multiple photo management apps simultaneously?
 Yes. Mount the same photo directory as read-only in multiple tools. Use Immich as your daily driver with mobile upload, and PhotoPrism as a secondary browser for its superior RAW processing and search. Both can index the same directory without conflicts as long as the secondary tool has read-only access.
 How do self-hosted photo apps handle RAW files?
 PhotoPrism has the best RAW support — it processes 30+ RAW formats via LibRaw and generates high-quality JPEG previews automatically. Immich supports RAW files and generates previews but with less format coverage. Lychee and Piwigo display RAW files if your browser supports them but do not generate previews. For serious photographers shooting RAW, PhotoPrism is the strongest choice.

 A self-hosted web interface alone is not the complete system. A usable deployment also includes:
 Original photo, video, and RAW files.
 A database containing indexes, users, albums, or recognition data where the application requires one.
 Thumbnail, preview, and transcoding caches.
 User accounts, passwords, sharing settings, and public links.
 Remote-access controls, HTTPS, firewall rules, and update procedures.
 Backups and a documented recovery process.
 That distinction matters when comparing software with Google Photos, iCloud Photos, or Dropbox. A cloud service normally combines storage, applications, availability, account recovery, and operations into one bill. Self-hosting separates those responsibilities—and gives you more control, but also more ways to misconfigure or lose access to the system.
 Which self-hosted photo gallery is best for most people? 
 Immich is the best overall choice for most individuals and families who want a close self-hosted substitute for a modern mobile photo service. The official project feature list includes mobile photo and video upload, background backup, shared albums, partner sharing, face recognition and clustering, metadata and object search, CLIP search, memories, map view, RAW support, Live Photos, public sharing, folder view, and multi-user access. See the Immich project feature list for the current scope.
 What does Immich do well?
 Immich puts the phone workflow first. A family member can back up photos and videos from a mobile device, while the web application provides a timeline, albums, search, sharing, and multiple accounts. Faces, objects, metadata, maps, memories, and partner sharing make Immich feel closer to a consumer cloud-photo product than a traditional web gallery.
 Immich also keeps a folder view, which is useful when a photographer or long-time archivist still thinks in directories rather than only in application-generated albums. Public sharing and shared albums cover common family and event workflows, although public links should be treated as security-sensitive credentials.
 What hardware does Immich require?
 Immich is not the lightest option in this list. The current Immich requirements documentation recommends at least 6 GB of RAM for a smooth experience, with 8 GB recommended; 4 GB may work when machine-learning features are disabled. The documented baseline is two CPU cores, with four recommended, and Docker Compose is required. Immich supports AMD64 and ARM64 systems, but older AMD64 hardware may need x86-64-v2 support or special version constraints.
 Keep Immich’s PostgreSQL database on local SSD storage rather than a network share. A media directory on NAS storage may be workable in some designs, but a network-mounted database is specifically discouraged. On Windows, filesystem ownership and permissions create additional constraints: NTFS and common mounted WSL host paths can cause database problems.
 Immich’s thumbnails and transcoded videos may add approximately 10–20% to the storage consumed by the original library. That overhead is not a reason to reject Immich, but it should be included when sizing disks.
 Who should not choose Immich?
 Immich is a poor fit for someone who wants a simple upload directory, refuses to maintain Docker and PostgreSQL, or has hardware that cannot handle indexing, thumbnail generation, and video transcoding. Immich is also not a backup strategy by itself. The project documentation warns users to follow a 3-2-1 backup plan , and the original media must exist outside the application’s only working copy.
 Verdict: Choose Immich when mobile backup and a modern timeline are the deciding factors and you are prepared to operate a real server application.
 Is PhotoPrism better for large or metadata-heavy photo libraries? 
 PhotoPrism is the strongest choice when cataloging, metadata, RAW files, and detailed search matter more than a phone-first experience. PhotoPrism’s documentation describes a workflow built around indexing an existing library, reading metadata, generating previews, and making a large collection searchable through labels, locations, faces, and technical properties.
 What does PhotoPrism support?
 PhotoPrism officially lists common image and video formats including JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP, HEIF, HEIC, MP4, MOV, WebP, and WebM for indexing, viewing, and conversion on its feature and format documentation . PhotoPrism also supports RAW photographs, Live Photos, EXIF and XMP metadata, and Google Photos JSON metadata.
 Search filters can cover labels, location, resolution, color, chroma, quality, and other properties. Automatic labeling and face recognition can help organize an archive that was never consistently tagged. WebDAV access, a progressive-web-app-style browser experience, and compatibility with phone-backup tools such as PhotoSync give PhotoPrism multiple ways to receive media without requiring a single specific mobile workflow.
 What are PhotoPrism’s deployment requirements?
 The current PhotoPrism getting-started guidance recommends at least two CPU cores, 3 GB of physical RAM, a 64-bit operating system, and at least 4 GB of swap. Large libraries benefit from local SSD storage for the database and cache, even when the original media is held on larger disks.

Compatibility with a platform does not guarantee good performance: a small ARM board may index a modest collection acceptably but struggle with a large archive, AI analysis, or high-bitrate video conversion.
