Original media may remain on your server while an ancillary map or geocoding dependency remains external, so “self-hosted” should not automatically be read as “every service is local.” Public installations should use HTTPS behind a reverse proxy such as Traefik or Caddy.
 Verdict: Choose PhotoPrism for a serious photo archive where metadata, RAW support, import flexibility, and granular search outrank the most seamless mobile experience.
 Should Nextcloud users choose Memories? 
 Memories is the best choice when Nextcloud already runs your files, accounts, and collaboration workflow. Memories is a free, open-source Nextcloud application rather than a standalone photo server. Memories uses an existing Nextcloud instance for storage and account management, so the complete deployment includes both Nextcloud and Memories.
 What does Memories add to Nextcloud?
 Memories provides a timeline designed for large libraries, albums, public links, map view, reverse geocoding, EXIF editing, and multi-user collaboration. The official Nextcloud mobile applications can automatically upload photos and videos. Memories also supports on-demand video transcoding, with optional VA-API or NVENC acceleration when the host, drivers, container permissions, and configuration all cooperate.
 Existing filesystem structure and EXIF metadata are retained, which can make Memories attractive to people who want a normal file tree alongside the gallery. Integrations with Nextcloud recognition and face-recognition applications can extend organization features, but the final experience depends on the installed Nextcloud version, mobile application, optional recognition apps, and transcoding setup.
 Why not just install Nextcloud?
 Nextcloud by itself is primarily a self-hosted file-sync and collaboration platform. Nextcloud can provide storage, sharing, mobile access, and account management, but a polished photo timeline, recognition, or video-gallery experience usually requires a specialized application such as Memories. The secondary comparison of self-hosted photo options is useful for this ecosystem distinction, but its pricing and feature claims should not replace current first-party documentation.
 Nextcloud is therefore a powerful private-cloud platform, not automatically the best photo application. If you also need files, calendars, contacts, office collaboration, and sharing, Memories can prevent a second silo. If you only want photo backup, installing and maintaining the broader Nextcloud stack may be unnecessary complexity.
 Verdict: Choose Memories when Nextcloud is already central to your household or organization. Choose Immich or PhotoPrism when photos are the primary purpose of the server.
 Is Piwigo better for teams and public galleries? 
 Piwigo is the best option in this group for structured publishing, permissions, collaboration, and gallery administration. Piwigo behaves more like a gallery and digital asset management platform than a consumer cloud-photo timeline.
 What does Piwigo offer?
 Piwigo supports albums, sub-albums, tags, metadata, search, photo and video content, public or private galleries, user and collaborator permissions, plugins, themes, API access, and bulk workflows. Media can be imported from computers, mobile applications, synchronized folders, or other organized sources. Those capabilities suit professional photographers, universities, public-sector groups, tourism organizations, nonprofits, and teams that need controlled collections.
 Piwigo can be self-hosted or hosted. The official Piwigo site says self-hosted users operate the software on their own infrastructure, can modify code and plugins, and can export photos, videos, and metadata. Hosted plans include infrastructure, updates, backups, and maintenance, but a hosted Piwigo service is not the same cost or responsibility model as operating Piwigo yourself.
 What is Piwigo’s main trade-off?
 Piwigo is less naturally suited to replacing automatic phone backup for a family that expects a continuously updating mobile timeline. Mobile import and synchronized-folder workflows exist, but the current application and codec behavior should be verified for the exact devices and videos involved. Plugins increase flexibility while also adding compatibility and update-management concerns.

 Is LibrePhotos a good open-source AI alternative? 
 LibrePhotos is a promising choice for readers who prioritize open-source local processing and AI-assisted organization, provided they are willing to validate the current deployment and media compatibility. LibrePhotos scans files on a filesystem and offers a broad set of organization features.
 What features does LibrePhotos include?
 The official LibrePhotos documentation lists support for photos, RAW files, videos, Live Photos, and RAW+JPEG variants. LibrePhotos includes a timeline, filesystem scanning, multi-user support, event-based album generation, face recognition and classification, reverse geocoding, object and scene detection, semantic image search, metadata search, perceptual-hash duplicate detection, slideshows, and public album links with privacy controls.
 That combination makes LibrePhotos attractive for an existing folder archive that needs automatic organization without sending the library to a commercial cloud. Face recognition, object detection, and semantic search should be described as supported capabilities rather than promises of accuracy. Recognition can miss subjects, misidentify people, change after re-indexing, and consume significant CPU, RAM, or GPU resources.
 What should you test before moving a library?
 Test the current installation process, update path, hardware requirements, and video codecs with a small representative library. Filesystem scanning is not automatically the same thing as a polished mobile-first backup workflow. Confirm whether the exact HEIC, RAW, Live Photo, MP4, H.265/HEVC, and high-bitrate files in your collection receive usable previews and play correctly on the browsers and phones your household uses.

 How much does self-hosted photo storage cost? 
 Self-hosting software may be free or open source, but the complete system is not cost-free. Compare the recurring cloud bill with the following total cost of ownership:
 Server, NAS, mini PC, or VPS.
 Hard drives, SSDs, and replacement drives.
 Separate backup storage and an off-site backup.
 Electricity for equipment that runs continuously.
 Domain registration, DNS, VPN, or remote-access services.
 Optional managed hosting and support.
 Time spent installing updates, investigating failures, and testing recovery.
 Replacement hardware and the cost of downtime.
 A useful comparison is not “free software versus a cloud subscription.” The useful comparison is cloud subscription versus hardware, backup, hosting, maintenance, and recovery costs . Self-hosting can become cheaper over several years when hardware already exists and the library is large, but a small library may not justify a new NAS, redundant disks, and off-site backups.
 What paid and managed options exist?
 PhotoPrism’s official features page displayed the following prices on August 18, 2026: Community free, Essentials €2.00 per month, Plus from €6.00 per month, and PikaPods managed hosting from $6.50 per month. The page labels Community, Essentials, and Plus as self-hosted options and PikaPods as fully managed. Prices are time- and geography-sensitive, so verify the current PhotoPrism plans before purchasing.
 Piwigo offers both Piwigo Cloud and self-hosted deployment. Hosted plans include infrastructure, updates, backups, and maintenance according to the official site; self-hosted users operate the software themselves. Check Piwigo pricing and the Piwigo self-hosting page for current terms.
 Nextcloud’s software can be self-hosted, while enterprise support is a separate commercial offering. A secondary article reported enterprise support starting at €71.29 per user per year for 100 users, but that figure should be confirmed against official Nextcloud Enterprise information before publication or purchase.

 For a small library, a capable existing desktop or mini PC can be easier to upgrade than a low-powered NAS. A NAS is convenient when it already provides storage, snapshots, user management, and a supported container environment. A VPS or managed provider is useful when reliable remote access matters more than keeping the server at home, but remote storage and bandwidth costs can become significant.
 Use local SSD storage for the database and high-write caches where the application recommends it. Store originals on reliable bulk storage, but do not assume RAID protects against accidental deletion, ransomware, application errors, theft, or fire. RAID improves availability; it is not a backup.
 Hardware acceleration is not automatic. Video transcoding and AI indexing depend on the operating system, GPU, drivers, container permissions, codec support, and application configuration. An Intel integrated GPU, NVIDIA GPU, or ARM board may work in one deployment and fail to accelerate another. Treat hardware acceleration as a configuration to test, not a guaranteed product feature.

 How should you deploy and migrate a photo library? 
 Inventory the library. Count originals, videos, RAW files, duplicate copies, sidecar files, HEIC images, Live Photos, Motion Photos, and unusual camera codecs. Record the existing folder structure.
 Choose storage. Prefer a filesystem with reliable permissions, snapshots, and large-volume support. Put databases and high-write caches on local SSD when the product recommends it.
 Create backups before importing. Maintain at least three copies, use two different storage media, and keep one copy off-site. Do not make the new gallery the only copy.
 Deploy on the LAN first. Create an administrator account and ordinary user accounts. Import a small sample and confirm originals, thumbnails, metadata, faces, albums, and videos before starting a full index.
 Configure secure remote access. Use HTTPS and a reverse proxy or VPN. Do not expose an unprotected application port directly to the internet. Protect the administrator account with strong authentication and restrict administrative access.
 Test representative media. Include JPEG, HEIC, RAW, MP4/H.264, H.265/HEVC, 4K or high-bitrate video, Live Photos, GPS metadata, face metadata, and sidecar files.
 Test the phone workflow. Check automatic upload while charging, Wi-Fi-only behavior, duplicate prevention, deleting a phone copy after upload, and restoring media to a replacement phone.
 Test a failure. Stop the application, restore originals and the database from backup, remount the media directory, and confirm that the library remains usable if the application is removed or rebuilt.
 What can go wrong with a self-hosted photo server? 
 Remote access exposes a security perimeter
 Viewing photos away from home means operating an internet-facing service. Use HTTPS, apply updates, protect administrator accounts, configure firewall rules, consider VPN access or rate limiting, monitor logs, and review public-link expiration and revocation. PhotoPrism’s deployment guidance specifically recommends HTTPS behind a reverse proxy for public installations because unencrypted access can expose files and passwords in transit.
 Video support is not a single yes-or-no feature
 “Supports video” can mean that an application indexes a file, creates a thumbnail, plays the original in a browser, transcodes it, delivers adaptive playback, preserves audio, or plays it reliably on a mobile connection. Those are different capabilities. Test the exact codecs, audio tracks, resolutions, and browsers used by the household.
 AI features are useful but imperfect
 Face recognition, object detection, semantic search, and automatic labels can misidentify people, miss obscured subjects, change after re-indexing, and consume substantial compute resources. Local processing may reduce cloud exposure, but biometric and semantic indexes are still sensitive data that require account protection and backups.
 Database-backed applications need database backups
 A database usually enables faster browsing, face search, deduplication, and richer filters. A filesystem-oriented workflow can be easier to inspect manually and migrate. Whichever model you choose, back up the database, configuration, and originals together when the application depends on them. A successful backup job is not proof of recoverability until a restore has been tested.
 Self-hosting is not always cloud-free
 Maps, reverse geocoding, email delivery, DNS, app stores, managed hosting, and remote-access services may remain external dependencies. Separate the question “Where are my original files and where is processing performed?” from the question “Does every supporting service run locally?”
 What are the best alternatives to the five main choices? 
 Lychee is a reasonable honorable mention for a simpler, photo-first gallery, but it is less compelling when the requirement includes serious video management and mobile backup. Nextcloud without Memories is appropriate when file synchronization and collaboration are the priority, not when the reader wants a dedicated photo timeline. Synology Photos and QNAP QuMagie are worth considering for owners already invested in the corresponding NAS ecosystems, where integrated hardware, mobile apps, and support may outweigh platform independence.
 Readers who want less administration can consider Piwigo Cloud, managed PhotoPrism hosting, or another managed deployment. Commercial hosted services remain sensible for people who do not want to patch a server, secure remote access, maintain backups, or perform disaster recovery. The privacy and control benefits of self-hosting are real, but they are valuable only when the operator can maintain the system responsibly.
 How do you choose the right self-hosted gallery? 
 Choose Immich if you want the closest current Google Photos-like mobile experience. Choose PhotoPrism if cataloging, metadata, RAW files, and search are the central requirements. Choose Memories if Nextcloud already handles your files, users, and collaboration. Choose Piwigo if you publish galleries or manage a team collection. Choose LibrePhotos if open-source local processing and AI-assisted organization are more important than the smoothest deployment.
 Before committing, install the leading candidate on a small test library. Import representative photos and videos, test mobile backup, inspect metadata, try sharing, measure indexing and transcoding, and perform a restore. A one-day pilot can reveal more than a feature checklist—especially for video codecs, permissions, storage mounts, and the recovery process.
 Frequently Asked Questions 
 Is self-hosting photos cheaper than Google Photos or iCloud Photos?
 Self-hosting may be cheaper over time when you already own suitable hardware, but self-hosting is not automatically cheaper. The comparison must include storage, backup disks, off-site copies, electricity or hosting, domains, security, maintenance, replacement hardware, and recovery time.
 Can a self-hosted photo gallery replace phone photo backup?
 Yes, but the experience varies by product. Immich is the strongest phone-backup replacement in this list, while Memories uses the official Nextcloud mobile apps. PhotoPrism, Piwigo, and LibrePhotos can receive media through supported workflows, but their mobile experience should be tested for the exact phones and backup behavior required.
 Is RAID a backup for a self-hosted photo library?
 No. RAID can improve availability after a disk failure, but RAID does not protect against accidental deletion, ransomware, application errors, theft, or disaster. Keep at least three copies on two types of storage with one copy off-site, and test restoring the originals and database.
 Can self-hosted photo applications manage videos?
 Most of the leading options can index or play videos, but video support differs by codec, browser, audio track, thumbnail generation, transcoding, adaptive playback, and mobile behavior. Test H.264, HEVC, high-bitrate, 4K, and camera-specific files before migrating the complete library.
 Do I need Nextcloud to use Memories?
 Yes. Memories is a Nextcloud application and uses an existing Nextcloud instance for storage and account management. Memories is therefore best for people already operating Nextcloud or people who specifically want its broader file-sync and collaboration ecosystem.
 The Bottom Line 
 Bottom line: Start with Immich for a family-friendly, mobile-first replacement for a cloud photo service. Start with PhotoPrism for a carefully cataloged RAW and metadata archive, Memories for an established Nextcloud environment, Piwigo for publishing and team permissions, and LibrePhotos for a hands-on open-source AI alternative. In every case, deploy privately first, test your real media, and verify that a separate 3-2-1 backup can restore both originals and application data.

 Leaving Google Photos is easier than the small surprises you miss. Seven Google Photos alternatives for desktop and homelab, from Ente to PhotoPrism to Nextcloud.

 An XDA writer went through what it actually feels like to leave Google Photos years after the move, and the honest answer was that the small surprises were the hardest part: the resurfaced photo from a decade ago on a Tuesday morning, the auto-generated collages, the album that quietly built itself around a trip. The rest, storage, upload, backup, search, is solvable with a desktop or a homelab and one of the alternatives below. We tested seven Google Photos alternatives across Windows, macOS, and Linux, focusing on the pieces most households actually miss.

 Why people leave Google Photos
 The single biggest push in 2020 was the end of unlimited free storage. Households that had built libraries of tens of thousands of photos suddenly counted against a shared 15 GB. Buying more storage is a fine answer, and many people did, but it made the alternative question worth asking for the first time in years.
 The second push is privacy. Google Photos ships trained on the library it holds, and although settings limit some of that, the underlying reality is that the images live on servers that also run advertising products. For anyone uncomfortable with that arrangement, the choice is either an encrypted host or a self-hosted service on hardware they own.
 The third is control. Google decides which faces get grouped, which collages appear, and which years get resurfaced. That is often delightful and occasionally weird. Owning the library end to end brings back the ability to say what the software does with it.
 1. Ente, best hosted alternative with end-to-end encryption
 Ente is a hosted photo service that encrypts every image, video, and piece of metadata on the client before it leaves the device. The desktop apps for Windows, macOS, and Linux run the same encryption model, so a home computer can back up an existing library or serve as the primary uploader. The server code is open source and can be self-hosted, but the default is Ente’s own hosted plan.
 The reason Ente wins on this axis is that the encryption is not a marketing checkbox, it is baked in. The tradeoff is a smaller feature set than PhotoPrism on the AI side, though search covers faces, dates, and locations well enough for daily use. Ente also imports directly from Google Photos, including album structure, which shortens the switch.
 Where it falls short: the AI search and auto-organization are simpler than PhotoPrism’s. On-device performance depends on the device, and older laptops feel it.
 Pricing: free tier with limited storage, paid plans for larger libraries at a modest monthly or annual fee.
 Download: ente.io 
 Bottom line: the right pick for households that want a Google Photos replacement without running a server, and want encryption they can actually verify.
 2. PhotoPrism, best self-hosted with strong AI search
 PhotoPrism runs on any desktop or homelab that can run Docker, and it is the alternative with the closest match to Google Photos’ magic search. It indexes a folder of photos, extracts metadata, runs face recognition, and builds a CLIP-style semantic search that finds “beach sunset” or “birthday cake” without any tagging. On modest hardware the first import is slow, then daily use is fast.
 Setup is straightforward on Windows, macOS, and Linux thanks to a maintained Docker image and a documented compose file. Storage sits in a plain folder structure that other tools can also read, which matters when the answer to “what happens if PhotoPrism disappears” needs to be short.
 Where it falls short: the CLIP search wants a GPU to be really quick, and mobile upload is not as polished as Immich or Ente.
 Pricing: free and open source; optional Plus subscription unlocks a few extras.
 Download: photoprism.app 
 Bottom line: the pick when semantic search is the feature most missed from Google Photos.
 3. Immich, best self-hosted with the best mobile uploader
 Immich is aimed straight at Google Photos’ core loop: a phone in the pocket that uploads new shots to a home server in the background. The desktop side is a web UI and a CLI importer that can push an existing library into the server. On any homelab or desktop with Docker it installs in about an hour and works well after that.
 The mobile app is what pulls people over. Background upload, incremental sync, and per-device folders that mirror how Google Photos organizes an upload queue. On the server side it does face recognition, timeline browsing, shared albums, and CLIP search, and it improves fast, several times a year the release notes are worth reading.
 Where it falls short: the team still ships a “not yet stable” warning at the top of the docs, so treat the server as one link in a backup chain rather than the only copy.
 Pricing: free and open source, self-hosted.
 Download: immich.app 
 Bottom line: the alternative to reach for when the phone uploader is what makes Google Photos work at all.
 4. Nextcloud Memories, best if a Nextcloud already exists
 Nextcloud Memories is an app that runs on top of an existing Nextcloud install and adds a timeline UI, face recognition, album management, and metadata search. Households that already run Nextcloud for files can turn on Memories in ten minutes without deploying a second service or duplicating storage.
 The apps cover Windows, macOS, and Linux via the standard Nextcloud desktop client, and the Memories web UI works on any browser. Search and face recognition are lighter than PhotoPrism’s, but the tradeoff is a single service to keep updated instead of two.
 Where it falls short: face recognition requires the recognize plugin, which adds a background job that a small Nextcloud host may feel. AI-style semantic search is not there yet.
 Pricing: free and open source.
 Download: apps.nextcloud.com/apps/memories 
 Bottom line: the sane choice for anyone who already runs Nextcloud and does not want a second service.
 5. Synology Photos, best if the household already owns a Synology NAS
 Synology Photos ships with DSM and turns a Synology NAS into a Google Photos-style backup target. The desktop client for Windows and macOS uploads folders and watches for new files, and mobile apps handle the phone side.  Pick Ente if privacy is the reason for the switch and running a server is not on the table. It is the least friction hosted option that actually encrypts everything, and it imports from Google Photos cleanly.
 Pick Immich for a self-hosted setup where the phone uploader is what has to work first. Pick PhotoPrism when semantic search matters most. Pick Nextcloud Memories to avoid deploying another service. Pick Synology Photos when the NAS is already there. Pick digiKam for a desktop photographer workflow. Pick Piwigo for a shared family gallery. Staying on Google Photos is still the right answer for people who value the auto-generated moments and do not want to run anything, and there is no shame in that; the choice above is for anyone the small surprises are not enough to keep.
 FAQ
 What is the closest self-hosted alternative to Google Photos? 
Immich is the closest match to the Google Photos experience because its mobile uploader and timeline UI feel similar. PhotoPrism is closer on search and organization. Running both on the same server is possible but usually one is enough.
 Can I import my Google Photos library into these tools? 
Yes. Ente, Immich, PhotoPrism, and Nextcloud Memories all support Google Takeout imports, and Ente has a first-party importer that preserves albums. The Takeout export is the safe first step, keep the archive until the import is verified.
 Which alternative is best for privacy? 
Ente is the strongest hosted option because everything is end-to-end encrypted before it leaves the device. Any of the self-hosted options, Immich, PhotoPrism, Nextcloud Memories, Piwigo, Synology Photos, keeps the data on hardware you own, which is a different kind of privacy guarantee.
 Do I need a NAS to run these? 
No. Immich, PhotoPrism, and Nextcloud Memories run on any desktop or small server with Docker. A NAS is convenient for storage capacity and always-on operation, but a repurposed desktop works. Synology Photos is the exception, it requires a Synology.
 Can I still share albums with people who use Google Photos? 
Ente, Immich, PhotoPrism, Nextcloud Memories, Synology Photos, and Piwigo all support share links that anyone with a browser can open. The link recipient does not need an account with the service.
 Are these alternatives free? 
Self-hosted options, PhotoPrism, Immich, Nextcloud Memories, digiKam, Piwigo, are free and open source. Ente has a free tier with limited storage and paid plans for more. Synology Photos is included with a Synology NAS.
